The Burgundians were a Germanic people who originally settled along the Rhine as Roman foederati, or allied troops, before migrating to the Rhône valley and establishing their kingdom in Gaul during the 440s. Under early kings like Gundioc, they expanded their territory and created a stable kingdom that balanced influences from both the Franks and the Eastern Roman, or Byzantine, empire. The Burgundians converted to Christianity relatively early and maintained strong ties to Roman law and civilization, making them less culturally alien to the Roman population than some other Germanic peoples. They developed the Lex Burgundionum—the Law of the Burgundians—a written legal code that blended Roman and Germanic traditions and profoundly influenced later medieval legal systems. This blend of Roman and Germanic law became a foundation for feudal Europe. The Burgundians created a regional aristocracy that became the foundation of Burgundian nobility, giving the region a distinctive feudal character that would persist for centuries. Yet their independence proved temporary. They fell gradually to Frankish expansion and were incorporated into the Merovingian kingdom; their territories later became the Duchy of Burgundy in the Carolingian system. The region of Burgundy itself retained cultural and administrative distinctiveness well into the High Middle Ages, partly due to the early development of local institutions that the Burgundians had pioneered.
